 Sell a Rental at 68 With a $300,000 Gain and Medicare Sends the Bill at 70. A Couple Jumps Three Surcharge Tiers for a Year, About $9,000, and a Property Sale Isn’t on Social Security’s List of Excuses. Here’s How Advisors Split the Gain Across Two Returns
 Vilma Rios Mon, November 16, 2026 at 3:07 AM CST 6 min read Quick Read 
 A $300,000 rental gain at 68 pushes a couple up three Medicare surcharge tiers two years later, costing about $9,000 for one year. 
 Social Security's SSA-44 appeal list covers events like divorce, a spouse's death or lost income, but a voluntary rental sale doesn't qualify. 
 An installment sale splits the gain across two tax years, cutting the couple's Medicare surcharges by about $4,600 and avoiding a $5,000 investment income tax. 
 Americans who work with a financial advisor have saved more than twice as much for retirement, on average. Find out what one could change for you: SmartAsset's free quiz matches you with up to three vetted fiduciary advisors in about five minutes. (Sponsor) 
 Picture a married couple, both 70, opening their 2026 Medicare premium notice. Their health and coverage are unchanged, yet each spouse's Part B premium has jumped from the standard $202.90 a month to $527.50. 
 voronaman / Shutterstock.com What triggered it was a rental house they sold two years earlier, at 68. This couple is an example composite; a hypothetical $300,000 gain lifted them three surcharge tiers for a full year and cost them about $9,240. Social Security won't excuse it. Here's how the trap works and how advisors spread the gain across two tax returns. 
 How a 2024 Sale Turns Into a 2026 Medicare Bill 
 Medicare's income-related monthly adjustment amount (IRMAA) sets premiums using modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) from two years earlier. For IRMAA, MAGI means adjusted gross income plus interest that is exempt from taxes. A 2024 sale sets your 2026 premiums. 
 Assume our couple usually reports $90,000 of income, counting pensions, retirement account distributions, plus the taxable part of Social Security. In 2024 the hypothetical $300,000 gain landed on one return, driving MAGI to $390,000. 
 ------ 
 Can You Answer These Three Questions? 
 Americans say they need $1.46 million to retire comfortably. Whether that number fits your life depends on three questions most people never work through: 
 1. How much can you withdraw each year without running out? 
 2. When should you claim Social Security? 
 3. How much will taxes take from your 401(k) or IRA? 
 A fiduciary advisor can answer all three using your real numbers. SmartAsset's free quiz matches you with up to three who serve your area.

 Story Continues At $390,000, the couple lands in the fourth band. Each spouse pays an extra $385 a month. For two spouses over 12 months, that comes to $9,240. 
 Each threshold is a drop. Going a single dollar over one reprices the whole year. 
 The sale also triggers another tax. The net investment income tax adds 3.8% on the smaller of your investment income or your MAGI above $250,000 for joint filers (26 U.S.C. § 1411(b)(1)). That threshold has no inflation adjustment. Gain on a passively held rental counts as investment income, so this couple owes $5,320 more in tax. 
 Why Social Security Rejects a Property Sale as an Excuse 
 Form SSA-44 lets you request a lower IRMAA from Social Security. Its list of qualifying events covers marriage, divorce, the death of a spouse, loss of income, and an employer settlement payment. The form also lists work stoppage, lost pension income and loss of income from property that was beyond your control (such as a natural disaster). 
 Choosing to sell a rental appears nowhere on that list. Social Security treats a voluntary one-time gain in modified adjusted gross income, so the bill stands. Once the spike year rolls out of the lookback window, premiums go back to normal. 
 IRMAA is only one of the surcharges that trap retirees who look wealthy on paper for a single year (we mapped the premium drop and the coverage gaps that go with them in a guide available at no cost: Medicare's Hidden Bills). 
 How Advisors Split the Gain Across Two Returns 
 The fix is an installment sale. Under 26 U.S.C. § 453(b)(1), that is a sale where at least 1 payment is to be received after the close of the taxable year in which it happens. You then report gain in proportion to the payments you receive each year (§ 453(c)), using Form 6252. 
 Suppose the couple closes in December 2024, takes half the price at closing and carries a note for the other half, payable in January 2025. Each year's return then shows half the gain, and MAGI lands at $240,000 both years. 
 IRMAA: They fall to the first tier, which costs $95.70 per person a month, or $2,296.80 per year for the couple. Over two years that totals $4,593.60, a saving of $4,646.40. (This assumes 2027 tiers match 2026's.) 
 Net investment income tax: MAGI of $240,000 is below the $250,000 threshold, so the $5,320 charge goes away. 
 There's fine print. Interest on the note counts as taxable income. The buyer could default. Depreciation you claimed on the property can follow its own reporting rules, so have a CPA map out the recapture before you sign. 
 Moves to Make Before You List the Property 
 Time the sale to the lookback. Income at 63 sets premiums at 65. A big gain taken before your 63rd year never reaches a Medicare bill. 
 Harvest losses the same year. Capital losses in a brokerage account offset capital gains dollar for dollar, which lowers MAGI right along with the gain. 
 Consider a 1031 exchange. If you buy replacement investment property, you can defer the entire gain. If you hold that property until death, your heirs get a stepped-up basis that can cancel the gain out. 
 State income tax on the sale depends on where you live, and some states tax installment payments differently. The right split depends on your other income, your filing status and how much your buyer is willing to finance. Run those numbers with a financial advisor or CPA before the listing goes live.

 The title "financial advisor" isn't legally protected, and plenty of people who use it are paid on commission for the products they sell. A fiduciary is different: they are legally obligated to act in your best interest .
